Chapter two of Francois Jullien's A Treatise on Efficacy unfavorably compares this writer's reliance on a theory-practice framework to the alleged lack thereof in Chinese works. He proposed that a "principle of polarity" characterizes all relationships in a field for which "coup d'oeil," or the ability to make accurate decisions under duress, is an integral part of "genius." That book emphasizes the matching of means to ends and the concentration of force on the opponent's "center of gravity." Ancient myths held that this substance was created after a beautiful woman was cut in half for practicing adultery. Folk rituals which use this substance involve mixing it with ashes of crops, and were carried out by shamans called Yatiri. A traditional form of interaction with this substance involved the use of lime juice. It was more popular in the highlands than on the coast because of its alleged benefits for respiration, especially in mining towns like Potosi, where it was used as currency. Both Bartolome de las Casas and the Second Council of Lima denounced this substance as a devilish pestilence, although its restriction only began in force after a powerful stimulant was isolated from it in the 1850s. Name this plant that is chewed or made into tea, a traditional element of Andean culture.

A forerunner to this event in fascist Italy was the battle led by Nazareno Strampelli. A similar program to this event has struggled to popularize NERICA. Cecil Salmon's importation of Norin 10 from occupied Japan was instrumental to this event, and the Philippine government cofounded the IRRI to aid it. The administration of Manuel Avila Camacho fostered this event with the help of the Rockefeller Foundation. Chidambaram Subramaniam partnered with M.S. Swaminathan to promote it during Indira Gandhi's rule, building upon the introduction of lime to the soil of Brazil's cerrado and of sorghum and Japanese wheat cultivars to Mexico. Name this massive increase in 20th-Century world food production from high-yield crops, which is partially named for a verdant color.

The Accordamento allowed this pope to fill vacant sees in Russia. A theological critic of this man was the author of the Janus Letters, Ignaz von Dollinger. Luigi Brunetti stabbed this pope's advisor Pellegrino Rossi to death, and a group of his supporters were called the Black Nobility. This pope beatified the Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan and rejected the Law of Guarantees, which stripped him of his temporal power after the Battle of Castelfidardo. His encyclical Ubi Primum defined the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception. This pope convened the First Vatican Council and defined papal infallibility. He also posted a set of eighty condemned statements in the "Syllabus of Errors." name this pope who ruled during 1848 and Italian Unification, the longest-reigning pope in history.

The speaker of a poem entreats this type of figure to trample the disenchanted "market of solace" of Grief-City. In a different poem, this type of figure emerges "dragging the puppets," causing the speaker to muse "then there's a play at last." The line "Who, if I cried out, would hear me among" the order of these figures begins the first Duino Elegy. Name these religious figures often discussed by Rainer Maria Rilke, who used the label "the dangerous one" to refer to their "Arch" variety.

Jacob Raz of Tel Aviv University claimed that an organization of this type held a human rights symposium in 1987 after a legal decision prohibited them from gathering in private buildings. The Guardian published sample questions from these organizations' entrance exams regarding the ethics of illegal waste dumping and the types of bank scams not prohibited by law. Members of these organizations semi-legally disrupt shareholders' meetings in an extortion tactic known as sokaiya. A majority of these organizations' members belong to the socially outcast burakumin demographic. Common punishment for members of these organizations involves the amputation of the little finger. Members of these organizations provided aid faster than the government in 1995 and 2011 after major earthquakes. Name this kind of crime syndicate which holds territory in Japan.

This film is mostly told in flashback as a group of men is trapped behind a false wall during a standoff. A former card hustler in this film is given an empty pistol and told to shoot a police officer as a test of his loyalty. Zbigniew Brzezinski claimed that it was key to understanding the contemporary situation in the Middle East, referencing a 2003 screening in the Pentagon. Its writer-director duo were Franco Solinas and Gillo Pontecorvo, and, while it shows the paratroopers of Colonel Mathieu brutally suppressing terrorists, the fall of the title city two years later highlights the Pyrrhic nature of the French victory. Name this film that depicts the struggles of the FLN in a North African capital.

This person was vilified by the non-French newspaper Aurora after being recognized while incognito during a concert at the Chestnut Street Theater. This person once declared that, though one's country is a secondary god, it is "the first and greatest parent," and also stated that people of sense prefer to go by the name of friend than the name of master. After a drawn out spat, a derisive nickname of this person was coined by Albert Gallatin. A document written by this person claims that "all Men would be tyrants if they could." This person's spouse was the subject of a 2001 biography by David McCullough. Her extensive correspondence with her husband includes a letter in which she tells him to "Remember the Ladies." name this second First Lady.

An abortive attack by this commander left a contingent of men under Thomas Troubridge stranded at the La Consolacion convent. In a literary appearance, this historical figure orders the death of a woman who pronounces "Damn them all," Eleanora da Fonseca. He went against the will of Fabrizio Ruffo by ordering the execution of the leaders of the Parthenopean Republic. This leader of a disastrous assault on Santa Cruz in Tenerife is referred to only as "the Hero" in a novel where he conducts an affair with the wife of "the Cavaliere." Susan Sontag's The Volcano Lover paints an unflattering depiction of this man, whose mistress Emma Hamilton was left destitute after he died at the Battle of Trafalgar. Name this one-eyed, one-armed British admiral during the Napoleonic Wars.

The downfall of a politician based in this city came after he feuded with Lloyd Stark, whose family fortune was made by popularizing red and golden delicious apples. It's not New York City, but Charles Lindbergh encouraged TWA to move their headquarters to this city, which served as the airline's hub until the 1980s. Two rival factions here were nicknamed the "goats" and the "rabbits." A shake-up in this city came with the revelation of the Insurance Scam. Count Basie played for six years with Bennie Moten's band in this city. A political boss based here ran the Ready-Mixed Concrete Company, notoriously ignored prohibition, and helped Harry Truman get elected to his first public office. Name this base of power of Tom Pendergast, some of which is actually located in Missouri.

A meeting which decided this type of event introduced a Commission of National Education and pledged to uphold the Cardinal Laws. This type of event was narrowly avoided at the Reichenbach Convention. An event of this type was the subject of the cartoon The Twelfth Cake and began after constitutional reforms allowed for the election of royal dynasties. Territory gained during one of these events was later consolidated as the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, and another was caused by the uprising of the Confederation of Targowica. The first of these events was reluctantly approved by a legislature plagued by the use of the liberum veto, the Sejm. Name this series of three events in which an Eastern European country was annexed by Russia, Austria, and Prussia.

Bernard Permoli used a provision of this law to challenge a fifty dollar fine he received for conducting a funeral in a church. It's not a fugitive slave law, but the Taney court upheld the validity of this law in Strader v. Graham. It was partially drafted by Manasseh Cutler. Cornplanter argued against continuing a war triggered by this law at the Auglaize Grand Council. That war ended with the Treaty of Greenville. A predecessor to this law mandated one square mile reserve for public education per thirty-six square mile township. It mandated the congressional appointment of a governor and created several population thresholds on the path to statehood in a namesake region. Name this 1787 law that incorporated the region between the Mississippi and Ohio rivers into the U.S.

This writer relates a hilarious anecdote in which a soldier named Artorius escapes being burnt alive in a tower by jumping down and crushing to death his friend Lucius. An enemy leader named Castor tricks some emissaries into coming close before throwing rocks at them in a history by this writer. This writer is the only source on a campaign which was led by Flavius Silva and which involved a giant ramp being built to a stronghold of the Sicarii. According to this author, it was at Machaerus where John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed. Controversy exists over the authenticity of this man's testimony on the crucifixion and his use of the word "Messiah" to refer to Jesus of Nazareth. After surviving a mass suicide, this man became an advisor to Vespasian. Name this Jewish historian who wrote about Masada and the sack of Jerusalem in his book The Jewish War.

The leader of this group legendarily survived a bombing due to the sacrifice of a faithful dog named Luks. The slogan "brotherhood and unity" was promoted by this faction, which executed people by throwing them into foiba sinkholes. This non-Polish group survived offensives codenamed "Case White" and "Case Black." Two short-lived republics were created by this group, named after the liberated towns of UÂžice and Bihać. This group carried out reprisals after the Bleiburg repatriations against perceived collaborators like the Danube Swabians. The Tehran Conference recognized this group as its country's legitimate government as opposed to the monarchist Chetniks. Name this group which sought to liberate a country later ruled by Josip Broz Tito.

An opposition leader of the Freedom Party during this period supposedly yelled that he may die, "but liberty never," when he was attacked by right-wing thugs. A statesman in this period offered to provoke his own assassination on a diplomatic trip to create a casus belli. This period was preceded by an era called the "closing curtain," during which the phrase "expel the barbarians" was popularized as part of the formulation of "sonnō" and "jōi." During it, the Sumitomo clan founded the first zaibatsu. In this period, Itagaki Taisuke and Saigō Takamori argued in favor of attacking Korea during the Seikanron debate. Its namesake won the Boshin War, after which he promulgated the five articles of the Charter Oath. Name this period of modernization after the restoration of imperial power in Japan.

A crooked politician named Lucius Piso was assassinated in this region. A bandit from this region came forth to claim a bounty on his own head, according to a story by Cassius Dio about the meeting of Augustus and Corocotta. A settlement in this region refused to accept Mancinus as a prisoner and accepted a peace treaty negotiated by Tiberius Gracchus. Mass suicides occurred after a twenty-year war in this region was ended when a city was encircled by Scipio Africanus the Younger. This region was once divided into provinces termed "Citerior" and "Ulterior." The city of Numantia was located here, and a major surviving landmark in this region is the Roman Aqueduct at Segovia. It was the birthplace of Trajan and Hadrian. Name this area in which the Romans founded Valencia.

It's not Jesus, but the birth of this historical figure is the likely subject of the hymn "O Come, All Ye Faithful." This leader's public support declined after he was accused of abusing his wife, Louise of Stolberg-Gedern. Before his defeat, this man's forces were demoralized by a failed night attack at Nairn. A song describes this man travelling in a boat "like a bird on the wing" as he fled disguised as a servant woman named Betty Burke. Flora MacDonald was arrested for helping this man escape during an episode chronicled in "The Skye Boat Song." Marshy ground caused a charge of this man's forces against the Duke of Cumberland to fail, culminating in a bloody defeat at the Battle of Culloden. Name this grandson of King James II who led the failed Jacobite rising of 1745.

The first book of Laura Kalman was a biography of this man, in which she alleges that the FBI possessed evidence of his homosexuality. He presented an affidavit by Bella Dodd as part of his publicity campaign in support of Owen Lattimore. This man was hired by an ex-navy member who had undergone shock treatment at St. Elizabeth's hospital, leading to his argument for establishing the Durham Rule for insanity defenses. The revelation that he had accepted a series of payments from Louis Wolfson led to his resignation from his highest post. This co-founder of the law firm Arnold & Porter was appointed to argue in a Supreme Court case on behalf of a man who had broken into a Florida pool hall, but was too poor to afford an attorney. Name this lawyer who was nominated but never confirmed as Chief Justice, and who argued on behalf of Clarence Gideon in Gideon v. Wainwright.

The death of the Fifth Dalai Lama was concealed from this monarch, although it did not prevent this ruler from eventually annexing Tibet. This ruler perpetually froze his country's land tax, which had disastrous effects on revenue after his death. At the behest of this monarch, Shi Lang was dispatched to conquer the Kingdom of Tungning. Jesuits were expelled from this man's country after Christian subjects of this ruler were forbidden from practicing traditional rituals in the Chinese Rites controversy. This emperor used the ethnically Han Green Standard Army to put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, and he is the namesake of a massive Chinese dictionary. Name this official longest-reigning Qing dynasty emperor, the grandfather of the Qianlong emperor.

In Letter IV of A Defense of the Constitutions, John Adams cited these people's political institutions as a precedent for the U.S. Constitution, and they credit the founding of their institutions to a legendary "White Lord." Strabo disapprovingly noted these people's "sort of woman rule," and a series of blood feuds among them was the War of the Bands. Because he refused medical treatment, a general of this ethnicity died of a bullet wound to his leg during the Carlist Wars; that man was TomÃ¡s de ZumalacÃ¡rregui. The root *haitz is the center of a controversy regarding their language. George Seagrave managed the hospital unit in a retreat directed by this commander, during which he was disappointed not to find supplies at Hanolin. In his most notable position, he was replaced by Albert Wedemeyer. This man debated the control of the X force and the Y force with a world leader whom he repeatedly dubbed "Peanut." He directed the lengthy siege of Myitkyina, during which he ordered Merrill's Marauders to undertake a grueling flanking maneuver. This commander advocated for the transfer of supplies via the Ledo Road instead of flying them over "The Hump," bringing him into verbal conflict with Claire Chennault and the Flying Tigers. Name this American adviser to Chiang Kai-shek during World War Two, who was nicknamed "Vinegar Joe."

The validity of long-term social causes during this period were criticized by Edward Keenan, who urged a search for political and cultural causes in a 1983 panel discussion. A public figure of this period became a Catholic in order to gain the support of papal nuncio Claudio Rangoni, and was posthumously cremated and fired out of a cannon. This period began after the death of a man nicknamed "Bellringer" and featured invasions by Sigismund III of Poland. Short-term holders of power during this era included Vasili Shuisky and three different men pretending to be a dead prince named Dmitri. Name this turbulent period in Russian history that ended with the crowning of Michael Romanov.

In a major diplomatic incident, this country's neutrality was blatantly violated when a crew from the USS Wachusett illegally captured the CSS Florida in this country's territorial waters. This country was the location of settlements such as the "Norris Colony," which is found near the city of Santa Barbara D'Oeste. Jimmy Carter visited this country in 1972 to see the grave of his wife's great-uncle. Plantations here which often employed slaves were called fazendas. The last monarch of this country invited Confederate cotton farmers to immigrate here but also managed to abolish slavery with legislation like the Law of the Free Womb and the Golden Law. Name this home of the confederados, whose last emperor was Dom Pedro II.

A city in this present-day state was originally named Strawberry Banke. The area that became this state was the southern portion of a patent whose northern portion belonged to Ferdinando Gorges. A charter granted by George III to a university here was upheld in a Supreme Court case argued by alumnus Daniel Webster. Name this state home to Portsmouth and Dartmouth.

John Adams claimed this practice was a "confession" to the inherent inability of people to manage the executive branch. This practice was controversially lauded in a history by George Grote. It was criticized by a thinker with a fable in which a herald witnesses a man cutting down ears of corn. A quorum of at least six thousand was required to carry out this practice, according to conflicting accounts from Plutarch and Philochorus, but it is generally agreed that people subjected to it could resume normal life within a decade. Name this practice by which citizens temporarily exiled people from Athens.

This text explains the entrenching nature of power by quoting Reinhold Niebuhr's statement that groups tend to be more immoral than individuals. It begins by expressing disapproval at being labelled an outsider, and it was written in response to a newspaper editorial named "A Call for Unity." This man was given a military command to form the Forty-Second Foot Regiment, which faced agitations by the so-called Malcontents. He devised an urban plan by which four residential "tythings" and four civil units surrounded each square, and he limited land ownership to fifty acres to support family-based farming initiatives. The development of this location was overseen by Paul Painleve and was implicitly criticized in the treatise The Army of the Future, which also derided the effectiveness of the citizen-soldier. Army Group C conducted a holding action at this place, which allowed Army Groups A and B to move north and then west in the sickle-slice maneuver. Its integrity was compromised once several tank divisions made it through the Ardennes Forest. Name this defensive barrier on the eastern frontier of France which did not stop the Germans during World War II.

A building established by a company founded in this country was used as a Gestapo torture house in Copenhagen and was targeted by a British air raid in Operation Carthage. In this country, a call for the government to replace cars with white bicycles was made as part of the White Plans of the Provo movement. This European country agreed to a truce in the Renville Agreement, and, in the early 20th Century, it adopted the Ethical Policy for the treatment of its colonies. A 1992 treaty signed in this country paved the way for the adoption of the Euro. Indonesia was a former colony of this country, which was ruled in the second half of the 20th Century by the queens Juliana and Beatrix. Name this location of the cities of Maastricht and Amsterdam.

This book links distrust in government to Yossarian's quote in Catch-22 about how the enemy is anyone who would get you killed. A People's History of the United States, 1492-Present

In the histories of this event, a man named Ernest Gill is the primary antagonist to the "Lordite" school of thought, which defends a leader criticized in an American investigation led by Senator William Alden Smith. Edmund Beaufort, the Count of Mortain, provided additional forces to this city's garrison under John Radcliffe. Along with Manck and Guines, it was incorporated into a namesake Pale by the terms of the Treaty of Bretigny. In medieval times, it was the only legal outlet for British wool being sent to Europe. Name this French port city on the Strait of Dover.

In one musical, a person with this last name repeatedly says that he is "F.F.V." and mentions family members like one who tricked the loyalist John Pyle into a massacre by impersonating Banastre Tarleton. This is the last name of the singer of a song extolling "the first family of the sov'reign colony of Vir-gin-i-ah!" and of a general nicknamed "Lighthorse Harry" in 1776. It is also the surname of a numbskull who "shits the bed at the Battle of Monmouth" in Hamilton. For 10 points: give this name shared by Richard Henry and Charles, which rhymes with "I'm a general, wheeeeee!"

The perpetrator of this event initially asked his former lover Mizzi Kaspar to join him, but she declined. Brigitte Hamann wrote a book about the perpetrator of this event in which she claimed that his syphilis infection precipitated this event. Gerd Holler proposed that its impetus was a botched abortion. A convent for the Discalced Carmelites was built at the location of this event, which was ordered to be burned by the emperor in its aftermath. Ida von Ferenczy was drafted to break the news of this event to Empress Elizabeth. Rumors that this event was sparked by a familial argument were spread by Otto von Bismarck. It led to Karl Ludwig becoming the heir apparent to Austria-Hungary. Name this 1889 disaster in which Mary Vetsera and Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria were killed in a hunting lodge.

A fictional member of this institution is derided as "a sneaky, booze-guzzling, yellow-bellied rat with a bottle for a brain" after accidentally killing a man. The morale of this group was the subject of the historian Guy Pedroncini's first published books. In a movie, several members of this organization are instructed to seize a position nicknamed the Anthill. A member of this organization faked a letter from Alessandro Panizzardi in order to frame a different member of this group. Colonel Dax serves in it in the Stanley Kubrick film Paths of Glory. An author blasted this organization in the press with the open letter "J'accuse!" name this armed service that experienced serious mutinies in 1917 and that wrongly accused its member Alfred Dreyfus of espionage.

Josiah Royce wrote a controversially unflattering history of this state. Eugene Macnamara advocated establishing an Irish colony in this present-day American state. Name this country once led by Kwame Nkrumah.

When he came to power, this monarch almost immediately named his illegitimate half-brother Archbishop of York, and he gave several of his advisors religious positions via the Council of Pipewell. Rumors claimed that this king killed his father, who had an affair with his intended bride, Alys of the Vexin. This monarch ended up marrying Berengaria of Navarre, with whom he had no children. He acknowledged Tancred of Lecce as king of Sicily to free his imprisoned sister, Joan, and he pledged to support Guy de Lusignan against Conrad of Montferrat on Cyprus. This king infamously massacred around 3000 prisoners at Ayyadieh after the Siege of Acre. Name this successor of Henry II, a crusader known as "Coeur-de-Lion."

It's not a naval battle in the Pacific, but this event resulted in decorations being issued to the crew of the soon-to-be-decommissioned USS Preserver. Boy Scout Troop 514 sponsored an American flag that amazingly survived this event. A speech given in the wake of this event stated "We've grown used to wonders in this century" and that those who died in it had tried to "touch the face of God." It caused the failure of the Spartan 203 Mission. Donald Kutyna received leaked information while investigating this event, which resulted in a televised demonstration of how rubber behaves in cold temperatures. The Massachusetts Supreme Court upheld the common law definition of this offense in the 1808 case Commonwealth v. Clap, citing its "direct tendency to a breach of the public peace." Canada similarly maintained the common law's placing the burden of disproving this offense on the defendant in Grant v. Torstar Corp. A piece entitled "Heed Their Rising Voices" touched off a Supreme Court case which ruled that this offense required "actual malice," denying damages to a namesake public safety commissioner in Montgomery. Andrew Hamilton defended a man accused of it because he had criticized William Crosby. John Peter Zenger was put on trial for this offense, for which New York Times Co. V. Sullivan carved out "public figure" exemptions. Name this printing of offensive, untrue content.

The Annals of Quedlinburg claim that Bruno of Querfurt converted a king of this country named Nethimer. Treniota led its Samogitian people to victory against the Livonian Order at the Battle of Durbe, and convinced his uncle Mindaugas to relapse from Christianity. The Peace of Thorn was concluded between the Teutonic Knights and a national hero of this country, Vytautas, who had earlier ended a civil war here by making peace with its Grand Duke, Jogaila. Jogaila's marriage to a neighboring country's Queen Jadwiga linked this country to Poland in a Commonwealth. Name this Baltic nation with capital Vilnius.

The line "Shall we count that a crime France counts an honor" was written about a British person of this profession, referencing an incident where a group of French people with this profession had pits and seeds thrown at them in London. A popular motif involved a person of this profession lying naked and sleeping on a couch. Many people began this profession by serving as "Orange Wenches." One of the first acts of the Restoration was Charles II effectively founding this profession in England with a Royal Charter, which legalized the employment of Margaret Hughes on Drury Lane. It was the profession of Charles II's mistress Nell Gwyn and of a woman depicted "as the Tragic Muse" by Joshua Reynolds, Sarah Siddons. Name this profession that sometimes involved portraying Lady Macbeth.

This leader appointed Bertha Wilson as the first female justice of his country's highest court. While in power, he married a woman thirty years his younger, who was later photographed by tabloids scandalously dancing at Studio 54. Documents declassified during this leader's tenure revealed that America had planned to invade his country as part of War Plan Red. During elections for his party's leadership, he described his plans for minority rights and urban reform as a "Just Society." This leader claimed that only "weak-kneed bleeding hearts" would be afraid to use actions permitted under the War Measures Act in an interview with Tim Ralfe where this leader answered a question with, "well, just watch me." name this Liberal Prime Minister of Canada whose tenure saw the 1970 October Crisis.

A holder of this position fathered the only Hungarian king named Peter. A particularly unpleasant person in this position attempted to secure power by marrying a slaveholding Lombard noblewoman named Waldrada and was burned to death by his subjects. A long-time holder of this position was exiled along with his son by the Council of Ten. The silver grosso coin was introduced by a holder of this position to pay for a campaign that sacked Zadar and Zara. The official vehicle for many holders of this position, the Bucentaur, was a barge from which they threw a ring into the ocean to symbolically marry the sea. A blind holder of it diverted the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople. Name this position of leadership by which Enrico Dandolo ruled Venice.

A historian who used this language is primarily known as "the son of a chatterbox," and Philip Hitti founded the modern American study of histories in this language. A person who wrote in this language wrote an eyewitness account of a ship burial by the Volga Vikings. A seminal work of comparative religion, History of the Hind, is in this language, as is a book that put forth eight principles such as "history is a science" to counter seven factors that make "all records, by their very nature, liable to error;" that text was meant to be the first chapter of a planned Book of Lessons. The main primary sources on the history of the Songhai Empire were written in this language. Name this language used in a book that discussed the communalistic sentiment of 'asabiyya, the Muqaddimah of Ibn Khaldun.

An account of this person's life contains the only contemporary mention of the war-goddess Andraste, whom this person invoked in a divination ritual with a hare. This leader massacred a detachment from the Ninth Legion under the command of Quintus Petillius Cerialis. According to Tacitus, the legacy of this ruler was invoked in a speech by Calgacus. Seneca the Younger caused financial difficulty by demanding that this leader immediately repay massive debts. Despite a will made by the king Prasutagus, Roman soldiers despoiled the lands of this ruler after Prasutagus died. This leader may have taken poison after being defeated by Gaius Suetonius Paulinus at the Battle of Watling Street. Name this queen of the Iceni who rebelled against Roman rule in Britain.

A princess of this dynasty caused a scandal after the trouserless John of Ostfriesland was discovered in her bedroom. The founder of this dynasty fled to the town of Mora and back on a route commemorated by an annual race and faced a peasant rebellion in the Dacke War. A monarch from this house was imprisoned by the nobility after he personally stabbed Nils Sture to death. A queen from this royal house abdicated after converting to Catholicism and housed Descartes in his final years. A king from this dynasty pioneered the use of field artillery, but died in combat at the Battle of LÃ¼tzen. This dynasty began after its founder's father was executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath. Name this dynasty that created the modern Swedish state.

William Ladd gave up commerce at the onset of this war, instead becoming a farmer and writing pacifist letters. An expedition in this war struggled to cross the Black Swamp after a militia mutinied over clothing rations. The United States financed this war largely through deficit spending by treasury secretary Alexander Dallas. During it, Alexander Cochrane tried to recruit the slaves of the opposing side by promising them freedom. A group of sympathizers in this war who warned the enemy about blockade runners were called the Blue Lights. A meeting during it called for a two-thirds majority to be necessary in Congress to admit new states or declare war and was the Hartford Convention. Name this war that included William Hull's failed expedition to British-controlled Canada.

Before the birth of this man, a seer has a dream in which he holds the sun and the moon in his hands and forces them to swap places. At the age of twelve, this man proves the irony of his name sounding like "fool" by killing seven hundred warriors, and he later kills two hundred men after they interrupt him playing the knucklebone game of Ordo. Like the main character of the Secret History, he is born holding a clot of black blood in his hand. Irchi Uul was a member of the forty companions of this man, whose wife Kanikei takes their son Semetei to Bohkara after his death. The thousandth anniversary of a poem about this man was celebrated in 1995, and that lengthy poem was performed in theatrical song many times by Saiakbay Karalaev. Name this national hero of Kyrgyzstan.

Several of these animals were beaten to death on the orders of Tian Chengsi after they heard music. According to Zhang Yue, some of these animals were trained to dance to entertain Emperor Xuanzong. In myth, silk production began after a girl promised to marry one of these animals, who was then killed. Sima Qian believed that the best kind of these animals came from Dayuan, and were descended from heavenly versions of them. Emperor Wu sent the general Li Guangli with an army to acquire some of these animals from the Ferghana Valley. The southern branch of the Silk Road is named after tea and these animals, which, in the Song dynasty, were purchased from Tibet. Name these animals which were used against China to great effect by the Mongols.

The outbreak of hostilities between settlers and this Native American tribe led to the evacuation of the Santa Rita copper mine for nearly forty years. The family of a warrior from this tribe was hung after failed prisoner exchange negotiations in the Bascom Affair. Their subgroups include the Chiricahua and the Lipan. The Camp Grant Massacre was perpetrated against these people, who were defeated by howitzer fire in a battle fought in a namesake pass. Their chief, Mangas Coloradas, was the father-in-law of their raider and guerilla captain, Cochise. The pursuit of a leader of this tribe was transferred from George Crook to Nelson Miles, who forced his surrender at Skeleton Canyon. Name this western Native American tribe led into battle by Geronimo.

A ruling handed down by this man specified for an election to be held in the church of Zion City to replace founder John Alexander Dowie. This man enforced the Elkins Act in a case involving the Western Stable Car Line and by slamming Standard Oil with a fine of over 29 million dollars for unfair shipping practices. In his best known role, he oversaw the resolution of a scandal that began when Eddie Cicotte threw an object that hit Morrie Rath. He refused exemptions on barnstorming rules, and banned "Buck" Weaver and "Shoeless" Joe Jackson for their role in the Black Sox Scandal during his tenure as the first Commissioner of Major League Baseball. Identify this American jurist whose unusual first name references a Civil War battle.

Upon being invaded by Sparta, this city repeatedly pulled a clever trick by telling the Spartans that they were violating the truce of Carneia, thus forcing them to temporarily withdraw. According to Plutarch, a king of this city tried to lure a thousand youths from a neighboring city into a massacre; that ruler of this place defeated Sparta at the Battle of Hysiae. Weights and measures found at the Heraion of this city are said to date to the reign of King Pheidon, who ruled this city as a tyrant. The organizer of the Seven Against Thebes, Adrastus, ruled over it, and it was the birthplace of a man whose mother was impregnated by a rain of golden light. Name this city after which the Greeks of the Iliad are named, the hometown of Perseus.

Robert Southey almost lost his spot as Poet Laureate in 1817 when a poem that he wrote about this person as a youth was published over twenty years after its composition. Thirty-two followers of this leader got drunk on wine and were subsequently walled up in the basement of a building, where they died. This leader's demands included the abolition of all laws except for the "Law of Winchester." Despite concessions made to this leader at Mile End, followers of this leader rampaged against Flemish merchants and destroyed the Savoy Palace. After demanding beer, he was attacked at Smithfield, and he was mortally wounded after a fight with William Walworth, the Mayor of London. Name this English rebel who rose up against Richard II in 1381 in the Peasants' Revolt.

A diplomat representing this leader gave the longest recorded speech at the United Nations Security Council, speaking for eight hours until collapsing of exhaustion. This leader established friendly relations with a northern neighbor under Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, though he later built outposts on that border via the Forward Policy. This leader's birthday is celebrated as the national holiday Bal Divas, or Children's Day. The death of an ally prompted this man to declare, "friends and comrades, the light has gone out of our lives, and there is darkness everywhere." Upon his nation's independence, this leader delivered a speech which references his nation's "tryst with destiny." name this father of Indira Gandhi and first Prime Minister of India.

This country's troops executed a maneuver named for the thirty-first anniversary of its army's founding in which they constructed a wooden footbridge named "Fatherland or Death." Troops originally from this country with the BM-21 rocket launcher helped win the Battle of Quifangondo. It provided artillery training to Guinea-Bissau's PAIGC, and a person from here advised the Congolese Simbas. This country sent a detachment of troops to reinforce the defenders of Cuito Cuanavale. It extensively supported the MPLA of Agostinho Neto, and it provides more medical personnel to the developing world than all G8 countries combined. Name this country that twice intervened in the Angolan Civil War and that pursued a policy of "medical internationalism" under Fidel Castro.

In front of this type of building, a British prime minister declared that the government was "shocked, but composed, and determined." Clementz Klotz won a contract to design this type of building, which was derisively nicknamed "The Colossus" because its massive scope caused it to be unfinished at the start of World War Two. Five people were killed in this type of building in an incident perpetrated by Patrick Magee. The Strength Through Joy program financed the construction of a building of this type on the island of Rugen, called Prora. In London, the Savoy is this type of building, one of which in Brighton was the site of a bombing that narrowly missed killing Margaret Thatcher. Name these businesses where guests may pay for bed and breakfast.

A primary account of this event includes a description of a "flower crowd" who eschewed putting slogans on their political signs in place of drawings of flowers. During this event, a group of African-Americans dressed as farmers and led a train of mules and wagons through the city streets. The essay "The Members of the Assembly" was written by Jean Genet about this event, about which he, Terry Southern, and William Burroughs were hired to cover by Esquire magazine. During it, a crowd of people repeatedly shouted "The whole world is watching." Julius Hoffman gave out harsh sentences to a group of people who protested this event, at which Jerry Rubin nominated a farm animal named Pigasus for the presidency. Name this party convention marred by the violent tactics of the Chicago police.

The city of Motyon in this region was captured by Ducetius, who ruled a barbarous speaking kingdom in this place. After killing his brother Theodosius, Constans II moved his capital to a city in this region. A great historical text in three volumes, Bibliotheca historica, was completed by a scholar from this place named Diodorus. Corruption and instability in this region were the causes of both the First and Second Servile Wars. On this island, a soldier bone-headedly killed a man who shouted "do not disturb my circles!" A heat ray designed by Archimedes may have protected this island's city of Syracuse. Name this triangular island located off the southern coast of Italy.

A ruler of this name and number established a bicameral legislature divided into the senate and skupÂština before his murder in the May Overthrow. A leader of this name and number used his victory at Slivnitsa to reunify Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia. Another ruler of this name and number was assassinated in Marseilles after establishing the January 6th Dictatorship in Yugoslavia. A ruler of this name and number annexed the Caucasus in the Treaty of Gulistan and declared a religious war that was crushed at Friedland in response to his forces' defeat at Eylau. That man's troops under Mikhail Kutuzov had greater success with scorched-earth tactics against his nemesis' Grande ArmÃ©e. Give this name and number of the tsar who repelled Napoleon's invasion of Russia.

A man whose nickname was "One-Eyed," John Monahco, was paraded and hung in the streets of this city. Violence erupted in this city after a group of its residents were kidnapped by Charles Knowles. The colonial history of this city is the subject of several biographies of George Hewes, and its occupation was the subject of the Journal of Occurrences. A vote to construct a new market here was narrowly won by the faction of Peter Faneuil. A series of battles to control it ended after cannons were brought to Dorchester Heights via the so-called Noble Train of Artillery. The ships Beaver, Dartmouth, and Eleanor were targeted in this city by a group of Colonials disguised as Mohawks. Name this city where a tea party occurred.

In the first of these conflicts, one side rebounded from a loss to the regent of the boy king Pleistoanax with a crushing victory at Oenophyta, but that side's fortunes reversed after an expedition to Egypt was crushed on Prosopitis by Megabazus. Sthenelaidas successfully argued for the initiation of a war of this name, over Archidamus II's pleas for caution. Donald Kagan wrote a celebrated history about a war of this name, in which the capture of Pylos caused one side to strand a contingent of troops on Sphacteria. That conflict, which was triggered in part by a massive naval battle near Corcyra, ended after Lysander caught the losing side's fleet unprepared near Sestos in the battle of Aegospotami. Name these conflicts between the Delian League and a namesake coalition that included Sparta.

An army led by this ruler obtained the submission of the historical Macbeth, as well as of King Malcolm II. This ruler's daughter Gunhild married the son of Conrad II, who transferred him Schleswig as a gift. Henry of Huntingdon recorded anecdotes about this man including his reduction of Gallic tolls and a probably ahistorical story in which he sat near the shoreline and commanded the waves not to strike him. Thorkell the Tall may have educated this ruler. This ruler's victory at Assandun allowed him to force a treaty upon Edmund Ironside, by which he acquired the throne of England. He was the second husband of Emma of Normandy, with whom he fathered Harold Harefoot. Name this son of Sweyn Forkbeard, the only English monarch other than Alfred who is called "the Great."

The first person to mention this city in writing was the Sephardic trader Ibrahim ibn Yaqub al-Tartushi. KÃ¶nigsburg was named in honor of the last ruler of this city's founding dynasty, who built its "Lesser Quarter" before dying at the Battle on the Marchfeld. Its founding dynasty was allegedly established when a ploughman with a broken sandal married Libushe. Vitkov Hill was the site of a battle defending this city, which was ruled by the kings of the Přemyslid dynasty, such as Ottokar II. A ruler of it built St. Vitus Cathedral and a three-towered bridge on which Jan Nepomuk was killed. Prokop the Great and Jan ÂŽiÂžka led followers of a Bible translator from this city against the sons of Charles IV. Name this home city of Jan Hus, the capital of Bohemia.

A novel about this type of event begins when Old Bundy is trampled by a horse and ends with the protagonist saying his last words, "let the rope talk." An instance of this type of event ended after a drunken revelry at the Combahee Swamp. The impetus for one was a Security Act that mandated carrying firearms to church services, and another is the subject of an Arna Bontemps novel partially titled after "Thunder." This type of event was planned to occur on Bastille Day by a man who had previously won 1,500 dollars in a lottery. A man alternately named Jemmy or Cato led one in the colony of South Carolina. Failed examples of them were masterminded by Denmark Vesey and Gabriel Prosser. Name these events that targeted white plantation owners in the Antebellum South.

A character claims that this historical figure is a "marshmallowy sort of creature" who "merely pretends to be bluff and crass and unbelievably thick and gittish." This person thinks that he is the target of two actors rehearsing a play about the murder of Prince Romero, and his father wants him to marry a rosebush after a fictional duel with the victor at Quatre-Bras. While trying to find a wife for this figure, this man's servant describes his mistreated, historical wife Caroline of Brunswick as having "the worst personality in Germany." He hired John Nash to build the Royal Pavilion in Brighton, initiating a namesake architectural style. Name this British royal played by the ahistorically thin and handsome Hugh Laurie in Blackadder who ruled on behalf of his porphyria-addled father.

A rebel leader in this country promised a "spring" to follow the "winter" of the Callimachi family's dominance of politics during its "Phanariote Era." This country achieved de facto unification under a leader who repatriated a quarter of its land when he "secularized" its monasteries in 1863. Its first king received the keys to the capital after the so-called "Monstrous Coalition" overthrew a man styled "Domnitor," Alexander Cuza. The Auraria Gemina Legion consisted of Hapsburg supporters from this country in the 1848 revolutions. Carol I of this country personally led troops in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877, which led to its independence, and it was formed from Wallachia and Moldavia. Name this country that ceded Moldova to Russia in the Treaty of Bucharest.

The first Queen regnant of this country declined to shield herself from the rain while attending the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, according to the custom that one must not imitate the person they are honoring. Shirley Waldemar Baker founded this country's Free Church and served as prime minister to the first king of this country, who took the name George. This country's first written legal code was promulgated from the town of Vava'u. This country brought a lawsuit against court jester Jesse Bogdanoff after Bogdanoff wasted the revenue this country obtained by selling passports to foreigners. This country elected its first commoner to serve as prime minister in 2014, ʻAkilisi Pōhiva. Name this Polynesian country ruled by Tupou VI, the only surviving monarchy in Polynesia.

A cartoon in Puck magazine showed a man with this surname as Sisyphus rolling a boulder with the word "Majority" on it up a hill. The town of New Utrecht was founded by a plantation owner with this surname. The first Secretary of Commerce and Labor held this surname. A surveyor with this surname drew the Castello Plan, which is often held to be the first map of New York City. The dying words of William McKinley were addressed to a man with this surname, who argued for increased government control over the money supply while serving as Secretary of the Treasury during the Panic of 1907. This is the middle name of architect Philip Johnson. Give this surname of the Dutch colonist Jacques and his descendant George, who managed the White House as the effective personal secretary of Theodore Roosevelt.

[Note: "Imdlawn Tashlhiyt" is pronounced along the lines of "i-mud-LA-win ta-shul-HI-yut, but English literally cannot conceive of the exact pronunciation].These people's calendar starts from the rule of a king identified with the biblical Shishak and is divided by four "Gates of the Year." Shoshenq I was one of these people, who are the closest living relatives of the Guanche. The Imdlawn Tashlhiyt dialect of their language allows any consonant to be a syllable nucleus. Gibraltar is named for a general of this ethnicity, the Zirid tribe of which revolted against the Fatimids. One sub-group agitated for the independence of Azawad in 2012, and members of the Sanhaja and Masmuda tribes of these people, who call themselves "Amazigh," founded the Almoravid and Almohad dynasties. Their Tuareg sub-group opposed Gaddafi during the Libyan Civil War. Name this family of indigenous peoples of North Africa.

D. Sefton Delmar's primary account of an event at this building includes witnessing a man triumphantly proclaiming "This is a God-given signal!" A plan to drop banners on this building on May First failed when they fell through its ceiling. A February 28th decree limited freedom of the press and suspended habeas corpus in the wake of an event at this building. It was shown in the 1990s that Yevgeny Khaldei took a photograph of a soldier raising a flag over its bombed husk. After an event in this building, Georgi Dimitrov was acquitted in a trial held in Leipzig, but Marinus van der Lubbe was pronounced guilty and beheaded. After the destruction of this building, a parliament was moved to the nearby Kroll Opera House. Name this German seat of government that was set ablaze in 1933.

This leader said that "Nothing valuable can be lost by taking time" in a speech that outlines the difference between a country and a marriage. Another speech by this man claims that the robber is at fault if he kills a victim who refuses to give in to extortion and states "Let us have faith that right makes might." He urged the "mystic chords of memory" to be touched by "the better angels of our nature" in a speech that repeats the sentiment that "We are not enemies." He gave a brief speech following a two-hour oration by Edward Everett. The line "With malice toward none, with charity toward all" begins the final section of an address by this man who also delivered the Cooper Union speech. Name this president who delivered inaugural addresses in 1861 and 1865 as well as the Gettysburg Address.

In 2004, Wal-Mart paid over 200,000 dollars worth of bribes to build a supermarket in this ancient city's archeological zone. Refugees from the eruption of the Xitle volcano may have been responsible for this city's expansion, and a man referenced in monuments in Tikal named "Spearthrower Owl" is thought to have ruled this city. The Wagner Murals were illegally removed from this city and depict its "Great Goddess." The talud-tablero architectural style originated here. In this city, the Street of the Dead runs from La Ciudadela to the Pyramid of the Moon, which sits at a right angle to the world's third-largest pyramid, the Pyramid of the Sun. The zenith of its power occurred around 450 A.D. Name this Early Classic Pre-Aztec site located outside of Mexico City.

This empire briefly tolerated its Jewish community thanks to the outreach of Rabbi Samuel of Nehardea. Vardan Mamikonian died in battle against this empire, although his successors eventually achieved autonomy from it. The armies of this empire included vast numbers of conscripted, poorly armored light infantry called Paygan. Ammianus Marcellinus recounts how this empire used cataphracts as their heavy cavalry. Despite being reinforced by the Slavs and Avars, this empire failed to conquer Constantinople in 626. This empire's greatest victory came after capturing Valerian, whose skin may have been preserved as a trophy by this empire. Name this Persian empire which overthrew the Parthians and was itself destroyed by Muslim conquest.

A forthcoming 4x video game set in this country combines turn-based troop orders with real-time non-player controlled combat, and includes separate happiness scales for peasants and nobles. A board game set in this country is an adaptation of Web of Power that involves scoring points for the placement of houses and emissaries. In Civilization 5, the faction named after this country can build a library replacement that generates gold and a crossbowman replacement that can fire multiple times in the same turn. A board game first developed here is played on a nineteen by nineteen grid of black lines, and players of that game use white and black stones to capture opposing pieces. Name this country where Go was invented, a popular weapon from which to feature in games is the Chu-ko-nu.

This character is disappointed that he is not allowed to bury his daughter with a book she had written her name in. In a different appearance, this character recommends Machiavelli's maxim about the escape of suffering to a man of low standing; later, at the Loyal Subject pub, this character learns that his rival had accepted a bribe of a silver cup that he then passed on to his servant. In a novel, this character's estate of Austin Friars is rocked by the death of his wife Lizzie and his two daughters in the plague. This man leads the persecution of the protagonist of Robert Bolt's play A Man for All Seasons, and he is the primary character of Hilary Mantel's novel Wolf Hall. Name this man who rose to become the advisor of Cardinal Wolsey and Henry VIII.

A 1951 general strike in this country became known as the "red sky days" on account of the number of buildings set on fire. This country's first independent prime minister led a Manual, Maritime, and Intellectual Workers' Union and maintained a personal army called the Mongoose Gang. In this country, Eric Gairy was overthrown by the New Jewel Movement. A coup against Maurice Bishop here led to concerns about the odd length of Point Salines Airport and the safety of students at the St. George's University medical school. During an assault on this country, soldiers were provided with topography-free tourist maps, resulting in the passage of the Goldwater-Nichols act. Name this Caribbean nation occupied by the U.S. In 1983 as part of Operation Urgent Fury.

The Yusuf Idris short story "Rihla" allegorically depicts a holder of this position as a corpse being taken on a road trip. The first holder of this position launched a coup in the aftermath of the unsolved Black Saturday fires. Missile boats under the command of a holder of this position sunk the Eilat after that holder of it promulgated the "three nos" and touched off the War of Attrition. The graduation cap worn by a holder of this position for an honorary doctorate in Islamabad was mocked by the television show al-Bernameg. Its first two holders were part of the Free Officers movement. In 2012, protesters against a holder of this position pitched tents in Tahrir Square. For 10 points name this position held by Muhammad Naguib, Mohamed Morsi, and Gamal Abdel-Nasser.

A political cartoon about this event shows a man with a knife being asked "Who'd suffer most if you killed it," referring to its title, "The Guinea-Fowl that Lays the Golden Eggs." A thirty-thousand pound donation from Australia extended this event, the central objective of which was called the "tanner." In its wake, membership swelled in an organization founded by Ben Tillett. This event arose over a dispute about "plus" money, which was paid for the speedy completion of work. It occurred in the same city as, and a year after, a matchgirls strike. The movement of New Unionism arose in the wake of this event, during which a wage of sixpence an hour was secured via the arbitration of Cardinal Henry Manning. Name this 1889 bout of labor unrest in the port of the British capital.

A historical figure who was killed for participating in this conflict is the protagonist of a 2010 novel whose odd chapters detail the last three months of his life in Pentonville Prison. A poem about this conflict compares a horse to a rider and then to birds that range "From cloud to trembling cloud." A person who was executed in the wake of this conflict claimed that he was hanged on a comma, is the subject of Mario Vargas Llosa's novel The Dream of the Celt, and probably wrote the scandalous Black Diaries. A poem whose title references this conflict twice mentions "polite, meaningless words" and three times repeats the line "A terrible beauty is born." Roger Casement was hanged for his role in planning this uprising. Name this rebellion that inspired a W.B. Yeats poem set in the year 1916.

Charles Neill was dispatched by the president to investigate this industry. Gustavus Swift made his fortune in this industry. Charles Eagan was forced into retirement because he defended the output of this industry, which was investigated by the Dodge Commission. Dial was spun off from a company that made its fortune in this industry, and it was the primary activity of the Union Stock Yards. Nelson Miles levied accusations that its firms provided defective supplies to soldiers in the Spanish-American War. Disgusting conditions in this industry are witnessed by Jurgis Rudkus in Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle. Name this industry of Armour & Company that drove Chicago to import large numbers of livestock from the west.

The narrator of Ernest Hemingway's "Banal Story" asks whether this person had two sides or a fourth dimension. Rayna Green used representations of this person to develop a cultural dichotomy in a paper titled after this person's "Perplex." Two months before dying, this person attended the premiere of Ben Jonson's masque The Vision of Delight. This person was held for ransom after being tricked into boarding Samuel Argall's ship, and, while kidnapped, Alexander Whitaker convinced this person to convert to Christianity. A possibly apocryphal account states how this person placed her head on top of the head of a man condemned to execution by her father. She took the name Rebecca during her tour of England. Name this daughter of Powhatan who married John Rolfe.

An executive in this industry, William Murrie, faced a sit-down strike that culminated in violence between dairy farmers and representatives of the CIO. A magnate of this industry stated "No man ought to be condemned to live in a place where a rose cannot grow," foreshadowing his patronage of the Garden City community of Bournville. The largest contemporary supplier of this industry is the Ivory Coast. A company in this industry distributed Ration D bars during World War Two, a conflict that spawned a competitor founded by Forrest Mars. A leader in this industry established a community fourteen miles east of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Name this industry in which John Cadbury and Milton Hershey made their fortunes.

In exile, these people were the first settlers of a place originally named "Elephant's Corner." Radical members of this group who followed Ã‰lie Marion were called "Prophets." The city of Privas was destroyed in an unsuccessful rebellion of these people, who were led by the Duke of Rohan. Several hundred of these people were massacred during the destruction of Fort Caroline. They were granted immunity from customs duties while fleeing to the lands of the Great Elector, Frederick William. Soldiers were authorized to harass these people under the practice of dragonnades. Guarantees of royally subsidized towns for them were removed by the Peace of Alais, and all toleration for these people was formally revoked by the Edict of Fontainebleau. Name these heavily persecuted French Protestants.

A speech that announced this program declared the three great evils as conceit, illiteracy, and bribery. This program reintroduced the gold standard by terminating the Kerenka and creating a new chervonets currency. A key tenet of this program was the reform of agricultural taxation with a tax-in-kind system called prodnalog. Its organization was one of the first tasks of the state planning committee, Gosplan. A political faction led by Nikolai Bukharin defended this program, which was opposed by Grigory Zinoviev and Leon Trotsky. The Kronstadt Rebellion hastened the adoption of this program, which was replaced by the first of the Five Year Plans after a flip-flop by Joseph Stalin. Name this program developed to replace War Communism in 1921, which relaxed collectivization in the Soviet Union.

The Battle of Conquereuil was a victory for a count of this region called Fulk the Black. A count of this region imprisoned Henry "the Senator" of Castile. The loser of the Siege of Berat, Hugh of Sully, was employed by a count of this region who had declared himself King of Albania. A count of this region gained an epithet from his fondness for the broom plant and married the former child bride of Holy Roman Emperor Henry V. A count of this region executed the last male Hohenstaufen ruler, Conradin, after the Battle of Tagliacozzo, which cemented his rule over Sicily and Naples. A dynasty named for this region was founded by a brother of Louis IX named Charles. Name this region ruled by the husband of Empress Matilda, Geoffrey Plantagenet.

This leader's response to the revolt of Sabbas involved questioning ten philosophers who successfully answered tricky questions like "what animal is the most cunning?" This ruler was presented a metaphor for government in a dry animal skin which only lay still when the gymnosophist Calanus stood on its center. This leader declined to join the voyage of his admiral Nearchus because he was too busy executing people like Polymachus, who had desecrated the tomb of Cyrus. The legitimacy of this ruler was questioned by a man who died after this leader impaled him with a javelin, although earlier this ruler's life had been saved by that man at the Battle of Granicus. Name this son of Philip II, a Macedonian monarch who conquered most of Asia.

The Supreme Court ruled that part of this bill was an unconstitutional bill of attainder after it required some workers to file affidavits that they were not members of the communist party. A year of strikes including a massive one by railroad workers precipitated this act's passage. Employers were permitted to file a representation petition regardless of election conditions after the passage of this act. The main groups affected by this act were unable to collect money through a check off system and donate to political campaigns. This act overcame a presidential veto. This piece of legislation was a revision to the Wagner act and outlawed the closed shop, thus permitting "right to work" laws. Identify this piece of legislation that limited the power of unions that was passed during the presidency of Harry Truman.

An act named for this commodity was used by LeicesterHemingway to establish an unrecognized country he called "New Atlantis". This commodity's presence on Navassa Island led to a border dispute between the US and Haiti, and slavery continued to be practiced in mines for this quantity by confederate exiles in the Caribbean after the 13th amendment was passed. This commodity's recent exhaustion in Nauru has led to a budget shortfall that is largely met with Australian aid. This commodity's richness in Phosphates led to its use as a "miracle fertilizer" in the 19th century. Name this commodity excreted by birds and bats.

One dynasty of this civilization was known as the Sealanders. In one ritual, the language of this civilization would be whispered in one ear of a bull, and the language of their conquerors in the other. This civilization was ruled by kings including Alulim, who held the throne for 28,800 years, according to their namesake "King List". One monarch said to have been discovered in a basket drifting through reeds as a baby served as cupbearer to a king of this civilization. Austin Henry Layard discovered the "Royal Standard" of these people's most important city. Cities of secondary importance to these people included Lagash and Kish. Name these people who established three dynasties in the city of Uruk, located in Southern Iraq.

This country organized the Salsipuedes Campaign against a native people who killed the explorer Juan Diaz de Solis. This country's group of 33 founding fathers are named for an adjective that remains in this country's official name. This country was riven for years by civil war between its Red and White Parties, and a guerrilla group named for an Incan rebel leader operated in this country. Giuseppe Garibaldi earned the nickname "Hero of Two Worlds" for intervening in a Civil War here. Name this country formerly known as Banda Oriental, which won its independence from Brazil.

This man fought on both sides of the American Civil War after being captured at Shiloh, then he was discharged from the Union army, and joined the Union Navy. This man grew up at St. Asaph's Union Workhouse in Wales before moving to the United States. The namesake of this man's boat, the Lady Alice, broke off her engagement to him and married another man while he was on assignment for the New York Herald. This man performed several secret missions for the International African Association, and his native porters gave him a nickname meaning "the breaker of rocks". Name this explorer, born John Rowlands, who famously met David Livingstone at Ujiji.

Don Alvaro Patiño instigated one war centered on this city, whose major economic activity produced both tacana and negrillos. Miguel Arzans y Urzua wrote the Tales of this city, and this city was the site of the Vicuña War. This city's site was discovered by Diego Gualpa, and development took off after the discovery of the mercury mountain at Huancavelica. The cerro rico was located in this city, whose mines were supplied by the mit'a labor system. Local Andean languages referred to this city as "the mountain that eats men" due to its high mortality rates. Name this silver mining city in modern Bolivia.

A rubber-substitute company co-founded by this man inventedgum after he withdrew his sponsorship and left his business partners with several tons of chicle. During one campaign, this man hid in a convent with his army and shot through the holes in its walls. This man launched a coup against his own vice president and held a state funeral for his amputated leg, which was severed during his service in the Pastry War. This man signaled his intent to commit the act he is most famous for by playing El Deguello, and during his final term, he sold land in the Gadsden Purchase. Name this Mexican General and politician who massacred Texans at the Alamo and Goliad.

A group of farmers in India did this after seeing water dropletsfloat in the air. The Treaty of Ste. Claire-sur-Epte mandated that one of its signatories do this, and Duke Mojmir of Moravia did this only to have his brother take an opposing course. At the urging of Frumentius, King Ezana of Axum did this, and a Sioux chief's son who did this took the name of Charles Eastman and co-founded the YMCA. Refusing to do this action in reverse caused the execution of King Ella of Northumbria by Vikings. Name this action that usually involves baptism in a local river.

This region's urine was highly prized as a dental hygiene product. One rebellion in this region was led by Viriathus, and the Saguntines were among the native inhabitants of this region. Emperors born in this region included Trajan and Hadrian, and this region was divided into provinces named for Baetica and Tarraco. This region was conquered for Carthage by Hasrudbal, and the city of Cartago Nova in this region translates to "New New City". The diocese named for this region by Diocletian also controlled the province of Mauretania Tingitana, and, unlike Britannia, this region resisted conquest by the Gallic Empire. Name this Roman region that consists of modern Spain and Portugal.

A group of aristocratic intellectuals called the jadids pushed for modernization in this country, and one Islamist movement in this country was founded by a former math teacher. That movement was attacked in the Andijan Massacre. This country's language is a modernized form of Chagatay Turkish, and this country faces a separatist movement led by the Karakalpaks. This country is the home of the Tughril Beg Madrasa. It's not India, but one insect-infested jail cell in this country's city of Bukhara was known as its "black hole". The daughter of this country's first post-independence leader, Gulnara Karimova, has been missing for years. Name this Central Asian country with capital Tashkent.

The "elliptical temple" is located at this site. This site was taken over by the Rozwi Empire late in its history, and a polity ruled from this site was rocked by a civil war between Changamire and Mutota. A soapstone bird excavated at this site is a symbol of its modern-day country, and this site was ruled by kings titled monomotapa. Building at this site stopped in the 18th century, just before it came to the attention of Western archaeologists who thought it was the land of Ophir. Name this site located near Harare, the namesake of a modern country.

It's not President of France, but one holder of this position died of a stroke suffered while committing adultery. Another holder of this position apocryphally held the "Banquet of the Chestnuts", and a third holder of this position was attacked posthumously in the synod horrenda. This position was subject to increased noble control during the pornocracy, and the last English holder of this position was Nicholas Breakspear. One holder of this position wrote Mit Brennender Sorge, and another wrote the Syllabus Errorum, which condemned basically every political ideology except conservatism. Name this position held by three consecutive non-Italians for the first time since the 15th century by Benedict XVI, John Paul II, and Francis I.
